meta.tagline: City of the polar night, the aurora and mountain-ringed fjords

overview.title: Welcome to Tromsø
overview.intro: Tromsø is an island city: colourful wooden houses in the middle of a fjord ringed by snowy mountains, holding onto the mainland by its bridges. The polar explorers set out from here, the fishermen sailed from here, and today people come from all over the world for one thing: to watch the sky turn green. From November to January the sun never rises; from May to July it never sets — in this city, light is dealt out by the season, not the hour. It is small, warm-hearted and, despite the polar air, surprisingly lively: the nickname 'Paris of the North' was not given for nothing.

local_word.definition: 'The dark time': the polar night from late November to mid-January when the sun never rises. A Tromsø local treats it not as a burden but as a stage — blue twilight, snow-glow and the aurora are this season's gifts.

rules.title: On the aurora hunt: patience and layers
rules.description: The aurora is not a show but a natural event: cloud, solar activity and luck must meet on the same night. Stay at least three nights, fill your thermos and count the waiting as part of the night — the best curtains open late.

rules.title: The weather changes by the hour — so should your plan
rules.description: You're in the middle of a polar sea: snow in the morning, sun at noon, storm in the evening is one day's programme. Book activities with flexible cancellation and don't mourn 'bad weather' — bad weather is often the best photo's backdrop.

rules.title: Don't underestimate the town — go out at night
rules.description: Tromsø is the liveliest city at the 70th parallel: the world's northernmost brewery, live-music bars and student energy. The night isn't over because your aurora tour returned — the pub culture is the cure for polar cold.

quick_facts.label: Aurora season
quick_facts.sub: Polar night: late Nov – mid Jan

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: English fluent as a mother tongue

tip.label: The Tromsø philosophy
tip.text: Here nature makes the programme and you adapt: clear sky means aurora at night, overcast means museum and pub. Think like a local — not 'what shall we do today' but 'what will the weather give us today'.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The centre sits on the island and is small enough to walk; the cable car, the buses and the tour minibuses handle the rest.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: The airport is at the island's other end: the Flybussen reaches the centre in 15 minutes, the city bus takes slightly longer for less. Taxis are short rides at Norwegian rates — the bus wins.

items.title: The centre on foot
items.description: The harbour, the cathedral, the main street (Storgata) and the museums sit inside a 15-minute circle. In winter the pavements ice over: slip-on spikes or lugged boots are a necessity here, not an accessory.

items.title: The Fjellheisen cable car
items.description: Four minutes up to Storsteinen on the far side: city, bridge, fjord and mountains in one frame. Queues form at sunset and aurora hours — buy the ticket in advance and go up in the evening.

items.title: The city buses
items.description: Buy tickets in the Troms fylkeskart app: the lines to the Arctic Cathedral, Telegrafbukta beach and Prestvannet lake work for visitors too. Cash doesn't fly; card and app do the talking.

items.title: The tour minibuses — chasing the light
items.description: Aurora tours sometimes drive as far as the Finnish border following the cloud map: choose operators with small groups, flexible routes and a thermos on board. Whale tours leave the harbour from November to January.

callout.label: Cable car tip
callout.text: Go up the Fjellheisen at twilight on a clear evening: first you watch the city lights come on, then — with luck — the aurora from the same terrace. Keep your descent ticket open-ended; when the green curtain opens, nobody wants to go down.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Tromsø you choose by the light: the harbour and pubs in the centre, the cathedral and cable car over the bridge, dark-sky cabins off the island.

local_word.definition: 'The ice sea': the Tromsø name for the Arctic Ocean. The city's identity was built on this sea — polar explorers, seal hunters and fishermen all sailed out onto the ishavet. The statues along the harbour are that era's salute.

items.name: The centre — Storgata and the harbour
items.description: The wooden-housed main street, harbour restaurants and tour departure quays: everything at your door. The aurora tours collect you from the hotel — the efficient base for a short polar visit.

items.name: Tromsdalen (over the bridge)
items.description: The side of the Arctic Cathedral and the cable car: you look at the city skyline from across the water and wake at the mountain's foot. A 20-minute walk to the centre over the bridge — a balance of calm and view.

items.name: Kvaløya island
items.description: 'Whale island': fjord shores far from city lights, aurora cabins and reindeer farms. 30-40 minutes by car — dark skies guaranteed; plan your groceries in advance.

items.name: Sommarøy
items.description: A fishing village an hour away with white-sand coves: turquoise water, polar scenery and absolute silence. Made for a one-night 'edge of the world' experience.

items.name: Prestvannet and the upper streets
items.description: Around the lake on the island's crown: walking distance to the centre but one step removed from the city glow. When the lake freezes, some watch the aurora from their own street — apartment and guesthouse territory.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Choosing a season in Tromsø is choosing a light: the polar night, the midnight sun, or the golden transitions in between?

items.label: Spring
items.name: White Spring
items.subtitle: Spring · Sun + snow + the aurora finale
items.description: March is the Arctic's generous month: daylight stretches fast, the snow is still deep and the aurora season plays its finale. In April and May the snow retreats, the seabirds return and the town rehearses for the sun.

callout.label: March tip
callout.text: The equinox weeks of March are the statistical peak of the aurora: skiing or a fjord tour by day, the light hunt by night — Tromsø's fullest 'two-shift' programme is built on this month.

items.label: Summer
items.name: The Midnight Sun
items.subtitle: Summer · No sunset from 18 May to 26 July
items.description: For more than two months the sun touches the horizon and climbs again: midnight mountain hikes, fjord tours and the sweet chaos of your sleep schedule. Green mountains, puffin trips and a day that never ends — a Tromsø without aurora, but a different one entirely.

callout.label: July tip
callout.text: Watch the midnight sun not from the cable car but from Telegrafbukta beach or the Kvaløya shore: at midnight the sun leans on the mountains, not the sea — the photographer's golden hour is midnight itself.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The First Curtains
items.subtitle: Autumn · The aurora opener, the whales approaching
items.description: In late August the sky darkens again and the first aurora curtains open; September and October offer coloured mountains and light hunts at once. In November the herring shoals enter the fjords — and the whales follow.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: September is the crowd-free aurora month: the lakes haven't frozen so the lights reflect on water, and the hotels haven't switched to winter prices. This is the photographer's Tromsø.

items.label: Winter
items.name: The Polar Night Stage
items.subtitle: Winter · Mørketid, whales, peak aurora
items.description: The sun doesn't rise but the city isn't dark: blue twilight at noon, snow-glow, and whale tours until late January. The peak of aurora tourism — book early and never skimp on layers.

callout.label: December note
callout.text: In the polar night there are 3-4 hours of blue light a day: build your daytime activities into that window and be outdoors between 11 and 2. No vitamin D, but blue-hour photographs guaranteed.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Polar cooking comes out of the sea: skrei cod, king crab, fish soup and the produce of the world's northernmost brewery.

local_word.definition: The migrating cod that arrives from the Barents Sea to spawn between January and April: the winter legend of Norwegian cooking. 'Skrei mølje' — served with its liver and roe — is the sacred plate of a Tromsø winter.

items.name: Skrei — the winter cod
items.description: In season (Jan-Apr) it heads every menu: firm white flesh, simply poached or baked. The brave order mølje — liver and roe included, like a local.

items.name: The king crab safari
items.description: The Barents giant is served steamed in Tromsø's restaurants; on safari tours you haul it up yourself and eat it the same day. Sweet, dense meat — priced like a king too, so order to share.
items.tag: In restaurants or on safari · for sharing

items.name: Fiskesuppe — creamy fish soup
items.description: A thick, creamy soup of salmon, cod and shellfish: the first remedy for polar cold. In the harbourside restaurants the bread is generous and the portions honest.

items.name: Reindeer — the Sámi inheritance
items.description: Grilled reindeer fillet or the traditional bidos stew: Sámi cooking's ambassador in town. With lingonberries and mash — the most local of polar proteins.

items.name: Mack and the Ølhallen
items.description: The historic beer hall of Mack, the world's northernmost brewery, has been open since 1928: polar beer from the cask, a polar bear on the wall. The town's warmest 'first beer' address.
items.tag: In the historic beer hall · from the cask

items.name: Café waffles and brunost
items.description: Heart-shaped waffles in the wooden cafés, topped with brunost or sour cream and jam: the official afternoon ritual of the polar night. Filter coffee alongside, snow on the window — this is how mørketid turns beautiful.
items.tag: Afternoon ritual · in a wooden café

callout.label: Budget tip
callout.text: The tour + restaurant combination melts a budget fast in Tromsø: solve lunches with fish soup and bakery menus, and gather the big meal into one evening. The tap water is mountain spring — don't buy bottles.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone rides the cable car; these six are the Tromsø that stays with the locals.

items.rarity: A mirror on the city's crown
items.name: Prestvannet lake
items.description: The little lake at the island's summit: a bird sanctuary in summer, a frozen white plain in winter. A 20-minute climb from the centre — above the city lights, the neighbourhood's own aurora lookout.

items.rarity: A cathedral scored for the polar night
items.name: Midnight concerts at the Arctic Cathedral
items.description: Inside the white triangular cathedral, midnight-sun and mørketid concerts are held: organ, voice and a vast stained-glass wall. The midnight sun concert is that rare event that looks touristy and fills with locals.

items.rarity: Polar swimming at the city beach
items.name: Telegrafbukta
items.description: The park-beach at the island's southern tip: midnight-sun picnics in summer, courage swims in winter. The local youth's barbecue shore — a city classic left off the tourist route.

items.name: The Polar Museum
items.description: Polar stories from seal hunters to Amundsen in an 1830s customs house: the wooden floors creak, and the stories are hard and true. Amundsen flew out on his final journey from this harbour.

items.name: The Sherpa steps to Fjellheisen
items.description: For those unwilling to pay for the cable car, a stone stairway laid by Nepali master builders: 1,200 steps up to Storsteinen. Climb it under the midnight sun — same summit terrace, better story.

items.name: Sommarøy and the Hillesøy coves
items.description: Caribbean-coloured coves an hour down the road: white sand, turquoise water, zero crowds. Midnight-sun picnics in summer, surfers under snowfall in winter — the Arctic's surreal postcard.

callout.label: Aurora tip
callout.text: If the tour budget is tight, build your own hunt: ride the city bus towards Kvaløya or climb to Prestvannet, load an aurora forecast app, and start the watch on nights with Kp 3+. A thermos and patience work as well as a minibus.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Tromsø's traps are not bad faith but the price-and-expectation games of polar tourism.

items.name: An aurora promise for a single night
items.description: Marketing that sells a 'light guarantee' to a one-night visitor doesn't even apologise on a cloudy night; the disappointment comes bundled with the ticket.
items.instead: Plan at least three nights and spread the tours across consecutive days; if you score on night one, the rest is bonus. An operator advertising 'free second night if not seen' is marketing in its honest form.

items.name: Expecting the aurora from the photos
items.description: Long-exposure cameras make the green brighter than the eye's; in weak activity the naked eye sees a pale grey-green cloud and the feeling is 'is that it?'
items.instead: Know the expectation: even at moderate activity the moving curtains are mesmerising, and on a strong night the sky becomes a theatre. Watch with your eyes; demote the photo to second place.

items.name: Booking a whale tour without asking the season
items.description: The whales follow the herring shoals: out of season (after February) the boats return from long searches, sometimes empty-handed.
items.instead: Aim for the November-January window and ask 'what's the policy if we don't see them?' The RIB boat is fast but cold; the big ship slow but warm — choose by your clothing.

items.name: Joining a night tour in city clothes
items.description: In open country at night it's minus 15, with wind chill minus 25: in jeans and a city coat you fold within half an hour, and your tour money melts into the dark.
items.instead: Build the wool base + fleece + windproof shell system; good tours provide thermal suits — ask when booking. Once your toes freeze there is no way back — double socks from the start.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Tromsø, invest your money not in natural phenomena but in being ready for nature: good clothing, a flexible programme and one extra night — that trio shows more aurora than any 'guaranteed' package.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order. (Winter version — in summer the midnight sun replaces the aurora.)

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From harbour to summit, from summit to the green curtain

steps.title: Storgata and the harbour morning
steps.description: Coffee on the wooden-housed main street, the polar explorers' statues at the harbour: while the town wakes in blue twilight, you're already out.

steps.title: The Polar Museum
steps.description: Polar stories from seal hunters to Amundsen: the shortest way to understand this town runs through this creaking-floored house.

steps.title: Fiskesuppe by the harbour
steps.description: Creamy fish soup + fresh bread: the polar lunch in summary. A Mack beer alongside if you're feeling brave.

steps.title: The Arctic Cathedral + the bridge walk
steps.description: Cross the bridge on foot: the triangular cathedral's stained glass is at its best in midday light. Photograph the city skyline from the bridge on the way back.

steps.title: Fjellheisen at twilight
steps.description: The cable car up to Storsteinen: watch the city lights come on, hot chocolate on the terrace. If the night is clear, the aurora watch starts here.

steps.title: The light hunt or the Ølhallen
steps.description: Clear sky: a minibus tour or the Kvaløya shore; overcast: cask beer and live music at the Ølhallen — the polar night is beautiful either way.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Town, fjord and sky — three shifts

steps.title: Classic Tromsø
steps.description: The one-day flow above: harbour, museum, cathedral, cable car, first light hunt.

steps.title: Fjord and animals day
steps.description: A morning whale safari if in season (Nov-Jan); otherwise a Kvaløya fjord tour or a Sámi day at a reindeer farm. A king crab dinner and a second aurora watch in the evening.

steps.title: To the edges, and farewell
steps.description: Half a day at Sommarøy's white coves: turquoise water and polar silence. A walk at Telegrafbukta on the way back, a skrei plate for the farewell dinner — and one last look at the sky for luck.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Norwegian's northern accent is soft; these five words work in the pub and on the mountainside alike.

items.meaning: Hello — saying it twice is warmer up north
A thousand thanks — close the tour, the plate and the directions with it
Cheers! — with eye contact, at the Ølhallen
The northern lights — 'nordlys i kveld?' (lights tonight?) is the town's shared question
'Oh dear / oof' — the Norwegian's lovable all-purpose exclamation; you learn it in a storm
